name: Wind turbine
seoTitle: Wind turbine Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Wind turbine: work out sweep area from the blade length and the height. A free ecology calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the blade length, the height, the wind speed and the turbine efficiency and the Wind turbine calculator solves for sweep area. That makes it useful for a footprint, a resource or an environmental change you want to size up. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Wind turbine calculator work?
sections.html:
The Wind turbine calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports sweep area in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the turbine type); then you type in the blade length, the height, the wind speed and the turbine efficiency.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Wind turbine calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Sweep area=PI × (blade length ^ 2)
Sweep area=(air density × area × turbine type × (wind speed ^ 3) − 2 × available wind power) ÷ (air density × (wind speed ^ 3) × (turbine type − 1))
Output power with losses=real efficiency × available wind power
Electrical losses (transmission)=(-real efficiency + electrical losses on turbine × mechanical losses × time out of order × turbine efficiency × wake losses − electrical losses on turbine × mechanical losses × time out of order × turbine efficiency − electrical losses on turbine × mechanical losses × turbine efficiency × wake losses + electrical losses on turbine × mechanical losses × turbine efficiency − electrical losses on turbine × time out of order × turbine efficiency × wake losses + electrical losses on turbine × time out of order × turbine efficiency + electrical losses on turbine × turbine efficiency × wake losses − electrical losses on turbine × turbine efficiency − mechanical losses × time out of order × turbine efficiency × wake losses + mechanical losses × time out of order × turbine efficiency + mechanical losses × turbine efficiency × wake losses − mechanical losses × turbine efficiency + time out of order × turbine efficiency × wake losses − time out of order × turbine efficiency − turbine efficiency × wake losses + turbine efficiency) ÷ (turbine efficiency × (electrical losses on turbine × mechanical losses × time out of order × wake losses − electrical losses on turbine × mechanical losses × time out of order − electrical losses on turbine × mechanical losses × wake losses + electrical losses on turbine × mechanical losses − electrical losses on turbine × time out of order × wake losses + electrical losses on turbine × time out of order + electrical losses on turbine × wake losses − electrical losses on turbine − mechanical losses × time out of order × wake losses + mechanical losses × time out of order + mechanical losses × wake losses − mechanical losses + time out of order × wake losses − time out of order − wake losses + 1))
Revolutions per minute=30 × tip Speed Ratio (TSR) × wind speed ÷ (PI × blade length)
Revolutions per minute=30 × output power with losses ÷ (PI × torque)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Open the page and it is already filled in. With the values it starts from — Turbine type set to Horizontal Axis Wind Turbine (HAWT), Blade length = 350 m, Diameter = 100 m and Height = 150 m — it reports Sweep area = 0.004 m², Sweep area = 0.0002 m² and Real efficiency = 25.8171 %.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Sweep area = 0.004 m², Sweep area = 0.0002 m² and Real efficiency = 25.8171 % should be roughly the size you expected from Turbine type set to Horizontal Axis Wind Turbine (HAWT) and Blade length = 350 m.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in meters
  • Area, opening in square meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Area, opening in square meters
  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Power, opening in kilowatts
  • %, opening in percent

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Wind turbine calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Sizing an environmental impact in familiar units
  • Comparing two options on the same basis
  • Putting a headline figure into context
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the blade length, the height and the wind speed — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Wind turbine calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns sweep area, derived from the blade length, the height and the wind speed. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Wind turbine calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the blade length, the height, the wind speed and the turbine efficiency, which is 14 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter blade length in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Blade length opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Sweep area = 0.004 m². Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Wind turbine calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
